landings.h1: Find the Missing Part — Animals — Kindergarten
landings.p1: On each row of this kindergarten worksheet a first group of animals is shown together with the total for the whole row, but the second group is an empty box. Children count the animals they can see, look at the total, and work out how many more belong in the box. Because both the part and the whole are pictured, a child can find the answer by counting up from what is there to the total, rather than by recalling a fact they have not learned yet.
landings.p2: Finding the part that is missing is how kindergartners first meet decomposition — the idea that a number like seven is made of smaller parts hiding inside it, such as five and two. It is the same thinking behind making ten, and it quietly prepares the ground for seeing how addition and subtraction fit together later on.
landings.p3: It is a gentle step up from straight counting, good for a small group who are ready for a little more thinking. When this feels easy, combine two full groups in addition with animals, or take some away in subtraction with animals. You can also browse every addition worksheet or the whole animals collection for kindergarten. Each one prints for paper work or plays online with gentle, instant feedback.

landings.h1: Find the Animals That Start with a Letter — Kindergarten
landings.p1: This kindergarten worksheet sets a target letter and fills a friendly scene with animals — some whose names begin with that letter, some that do not. The child finds and marks every animal whose name starts with the chosen letter, such as a cat, a cow and a camel for the letter C, then counts how many they found. Other animals are mixed in on purpose, so the child has to listen for the starting sound of each name rather than simply pointing at any picture.
landings.p2: Although it lives among the counting worksheets, the real work here is the link between a letter and the sound a word starts with — matching the printed letter to the first sound of each animal's name. That beginning-sound awareness is one of the first reading-readiness skills, and the counting at the end gives it a satisfying, low-pressure finish.
landings.p3: It works best chosen to match the letter a class is learning that week, so the hunt reinforces the lesson. When the hunt is done, count and combine in addition with animals, or make a graph in picture graph with animals. You can also browse every letter hunt worksheet or the whole animals collection for kindergarten.

landings.h1: Addition with Fourth of July Things — Kindergarten
landings.p1: This kindergarten worksheet sets out two small groups of flags, stars and a drum on each row, with a plus sign between them and an empty box after the equals sign. Children count the Fourth of July things in the first group, count the second group, and write how many there are in all. A row might pair a few with a couple more, so the same skill comes back with a fresh picture each time. The pictures carry the whole problem, so a child who cannot yet read a written equation can still solve every line by touching and counting what is there.
landings.p2: Counting two groups and then saying how many there are in all is the first real step into addition. Long before a symbol means anything, a child who combines one pile of Fourth of July things with another and recounts the whole set is already adding — and keeping totals within ten means every answer can be checked by counting rather than guessed.
